Collaborative Fund Conversations: Matt Sonsini

 SHARE ↓

 Copy Link
 

 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 The limits of good intentions: Matt Sonsini on philanthropy’s feedback problem, startup term sheets, and learning to be an optimist.

 🎙️ Listen on Spotify , Apple , or wherever you get your podcasts. 

 Matt Sonsini is Managing Partner and co-founder of Ravello Impact, and the former CEO of The Sobrato Organization. Before moving into investing and philanthropy, he spent almost two decades as a corporate lawyer in Silicon Valley, working with startups, venture capitalists, and public companies.

 In this conversation, he explains why waiting to give can become its own excuse, why measuring philanthropic impact is harder than measuring investment returns, and what founders sacrifice when they chase the highest valuation. He also revisits the boardroom moment when a CEO quit on the spot and the unlikely IPO that still stands out decades later.

 
 “Well, I guess if you’re Warren Buffett, you have a reasonable shot at compounding capital at a greater rate than the world’s problems are compounding. But for mere mortal investors, I’m personally doubtful that’s the case.”

 

 Key Takeaways:

 
 
 Giving has its own risk-return spectrum : Local food banks offer immediate, measurable results. Systemic change demands more time, more resources, and a willingness to accept uncertain outcomes. Sonsini approaches those choices as a portfolio, allocating across both.

 

 
 Good intentions need honest feedback : A business with a bad product hears from the market. A donor can still get a gala and a name on a building without knowing how much good the money did. He also argues that funders, nonprofits, and government need to collaborate more to make their resources count.

 

 
 A higher valuation can hide a worse deal : Senior liquidation preferences and separate investor approval rights can create conflicts when growth stalls. He urges founders to resist trading away important terms to reach a headline valuation.

 

 
 Venture’s failures are part of the process : Funding booms draw talent and ideas into new markets. Many companies fail in the correction, but investors cannot know the eventual winners in advance. He sees that experimentation as necessary.

 

 
 Optimism takes practice : Legal training taught Sonsini to look for downside. Investing taught him that optimism is essential. The best advisers, he says, tell clients which risks matter and which they can stop worrying about.

principles.title: The Sublime Experience of Reading | Robert Greene
principles.content: You know, music can get you to a sublime place. I don't want to say easily, but there's something I think very powerful and primal about music. Like a few notes can can touch you in a very deep place musically. But I I feel as a writer, but also someone who loves literature, that it's harder to do with litera- like the sheer skill and mastery it takes to transport someone in sentences or pages, >> Uh-huh. >> especially to a thing that you don't know anything about. That's why I think I was so struck by Death Comes for the Archbishop. Like it should have been it should be a boring book. Like nothing happens. Like this guy >> I read it when I was in my 20s. I hardly remember, but I remember loving it. >> about a priest being assigned to the Southwest. Yeah. And And it's not like a Cormac McCarthy novel where it's just like one disturbing violent encounter after another. It's It's kind of cerebral and slow and spiritual. And just when you read writing that so perfectly nails whatever it's communicating and you get lost and immersed in it, it's just it's a magical thing. >> Yeah. I mean, I'm in this process where I'm rereading books that were had a very big influence on me in my 20s. I don't really know why. Um and I was reading this rereading a novel by Dostoevsky's probably my my favorite novelist. And um it's it's about uh these nihilists in Russia who end up turning into like what would turn into the Russian Revolution. And it's so perfectly captures the moment. So I have this thing in in the sublime book. It was a word that kept coming to me and I was going to use it in the book, but I never did. And the word was just there. And I felt like I would read a book and I was there. >> Mm. >> I would read about history and I was there. I was actually experiencing what people were experiencing or biography and I was there or a great novel. I'm inside it. I 'm there. And so it's a it's a confluence of [snorts] a great writer, but it's also your spirit that that you have to bring into it and you have to I talked about that in one of my chapters about how you approach literature. I had a story in there from Franz Kafka, a very unknown story called The Burrow, um where it's just from the point of view of a of a mole in a burrow >> Yeah. >> and his anxiety. And you're reading it and you and and like mole. By the end of the story, 80 pages long, you are you feel like you are the mole in this burrow. It's so intense that he's about there's some beast trying to get into his burrow that he's made so comfortable. You feel like you've become this mole that's so so afraid of everything, like how we're all so fearful and anxious in our little spaces. And it's his masterful writing, but you have to like get over the sense of this is ridiculous. I am not a mole. You have to just your spirit has to enter into the what this person the magic this person is weaving. So you were able with Willa Cather to kind of enter into that world and that's what made this a sublime moment. A reader who's just reading it and just seeing facts and it's about New Mexico it's nothing to do with my life. Oh my god, it's not relevant cuz so many people they read books, they see films and it all has to be a narcissistic reflection of their own tastes and desires. >> Right. >> What does a priest dying in 1830 makes have to do with my life here now with all of my problems in social media? You got to get out of your little petty world and enter into other worlds and that what what makes a literature or anything sublime. >> Isn't that the the whole point of reading too? It's like reading is a form of magic. It's time travel. It allows you to it sort of spirit hop into different lives, into different moments, into into places you would never actually want to go. >> Yeah. >> And I mean the founding of Stoicism is built around this this prophecy that Zeno gets from the Oracle at Delphi who says that the good life is having conversations with the dead. And that that's what reading is, that you can embody a priest in New Mexico in the 1830s, or you can embody a mole, or you can embody you know, great historical writing and great fiction allow you to transport yourself >> Yeah. >> to a different time and place. >> Well, most definitely. I I mean, I just remember thinking about myself and my childhood. You know, I grew up in Los Angeles in kind of a boring neighborhood, you know, what is now Brentwood. And I felt very alienated. Like it wasn't comfortable to me. It wasn't the world that I felt that you know, I was a part of. >> Mm. >> You know, and I had to go to like Hebrew school and learn Hebrew and had nothing to do with my life. And I discovered books. And the books just took me into these other worlds, right? And I became addicted. And I'm talking about eight years old, you know? And I started ordering like hundreds of these tiny little paperback books that you could get for like a nickel, right? It just drove my parents crazy. And I just read and read and read and entered all of these worlds, and it saved my life. I wouldn't be here talking to you, Ryan Holiday, if I hadn't gone through that. It enriched It It made me who I am, being able to transport myself out of this narrow little world that I grew up in into something vast, human history for 50,000 years, however however when you want to start it, is this insane story. It's the most amazing, incredible story, our history, our past, our ancestry. There are millions of these incredible stories out there, and even the most boring ones are interesting because it's the past. It's people who were different from us. And you have all of this opportunity as a human being. You only have 70, 80 years to live, perhaps. You should be entering all of these worlds because it just it makes you human, I believe. >> Yeah, we have a a poem on the window of the bookstore from Margaret Engle, and she says um books are door shaped, like that the Yeah, they're they're This is a door. It 's like a portal. A book is a portal into another time and place. And what a minuscule percentage of the population walks through those doors. And then there is something special as you said about walking through the door multiple times. Like how we don't step in the same river twice. Like when you come back to a book and you see the things that struck you before or that are striking you for a new time that you just you just couldn't have appreciated the first time. >> I'll give you an example. I read a book researching for this one about the Aztecs and it was called Aztec Philosophy and it was about 800 pages thick. And a little bit like the Will of Cather book, there were so many details it was on the surface quite boring >> Yeah. >> because he goes into all the little details of how they thought and how they thought in terms of shapes and patterns. And suddenly I start getting it and it's absolutely fascinating. But the the point I'm trying to make is it's so completely different from Western thinking, right? Like for the Aztecs, the sun was the center of their universe, right? And they believed that the sun was died and then was born again so that they were now living in the period of the fifth sun. And um so you get caught up into this world that is so alien from your own. And yet it's not that alien because they're human, right? And you can still kind of relate to it. And so I'm absorbing all this information and I start thinking. I started going out in the world and looking at the sun differently. I'm starting to see kind of the patterns. So my point is we're so locked into this 21st century way of thinking. It's like a prison. >> Yeah. >> And it's getting narrow and narrow and narrow with through social media. This is how you're supposed to think. This is what reality is. And books take you out of that little narrow prison that we all live in in the in the present moment and they expose you to different ways of thinking, different ways of relating and it just enriches you and it opens your mind up to all these different >> Have you read the Under the Jaguar Sun by Talo Calvino? >> No. >> He wrote these series of essays, like one on each sense, one on sight, one on smell. >> that. Yeah, yeah. >> And one is about he's touring these like Aztec sites in in in Mexico or South America or something and he's basically imagining what it's like to be sacrificed on a pagan altar and how the person isn't like afraid but like empowered like they're enjoying it and then he's comparing it to like he he has this kind of theory that like maybe that's why the food was so spicy was because like they were eating the human flesh and they needed to come up with ways to like make it not taste terrible. And then so, you know, you have Mexican food six months later and some passage from this book flashes in your mind and and it it changes the experience. And then he has this other essay where it's like what it's like to be sitting on a throne, like a a semi-modern throne of a of an authoritarian ruler who's hearing this tapping from a dungeon below, kind of like a sword of Damocles. >> Oh, it sounds like an amazing book. >> It's incredible. And and it's just like I would never have been able to empathize with what it's like to be Vladimir Putin or Kim Jong Un or, you know, some king or even Nero. And And you're just like, how did he do this? This is magic. This is a superpower. And And And you're in that world. And even if just a a tiny bit of that residue stays with you, it it makes the rest of your life less ordinary. >> Yeah, yeah. Oh, it's a fantastic book. I have to I have to get a copy. I wish you had told me that when I was writing research for this book. >> it I read it two months ago. I read it two months ago. But But probably But then probably the reason it struck me is because I had read your book not long before that. Like that's what's so powerful about reading is it's not just the book but it's how the books stack up and in what order you read them and how I done them in the other order maybe I would have >> Yeah. >> Sometimes I read especially I was Samantha just recommended this book to me and and I was like I I'm actually having trouble with it. So many of the sentences are good. I have to stop. Like I can't just read this mindlessly. It's called the Emerald Mile and it's about these people who are trying to set the record rafting through the Grand Canyon at the the fastest speed that it's ever done. And again there's this there's these passages where they he's just sort of waxing philosophically on like how the Grand Canyon was formed and and you would like this cuz it connected I thought of your book too Coronado's expedition. I think it's Coronado. One of the Spanish conquistadors sees the Grand Canyon and they know that they see it and they basically write nothing of it. He writes about like we discovered jackrabbits and all these sort of banal observations and then they say nothing about the Grand Canyon. >> Why? >> The author's theory was that they literally just could not comprehend it. Like imagine it's the 1500s. You can't comprehend something being millions of years old. They can't they don't even have like the perspective to understand how big it is and and it was just basically it just goes right over their head. >> Or maybe they were just so overwhelmed they couldn't even begin to describe it or they wanted to keep it a secret. I don't know. >> It goes to your point which is that you can lead a horse to a sublime experience, but you can't make them drink it in.

principles.title: The Impossible Speed of Elon Musk -  Ex-Tesla President
principles.content: I think you scaled Tesla about 10x while you were there. >> Yeah, literally the physics were impossible. Elon turns to me on a Monday and says, "Marketing budget here is precisely zero and you need to double the company every 6 to 8 months." He believes that speed of all types, speed of decision-m, speed of cash through the business creates decadel long advantages. If you were to create a cheat sheet for decision-m, what would be on it? >> First step would be begin with the end. What is the outcome that you want? Step two is what would need to be true for that outcome. Then third step is what did you learn about communicating with Elon that was different? Most organizations you go up the hierarchy with your question and it comes back down and it looks like an EKG. Elon was like let's make it look like a dead patient. If you need an answer, go to the person that has that answer. Don't go through their boss or their boss's boss. Second key that he said all the time was give me bad news as fast as you know about it. Cuz bad news only gets worse with time. >> How did you know it was time to leave Tesla? What was your first meeting with Elon? Like first meeting was uh in person was at SpaceX. So it was for this like tech nerd. It was pretty awesome to walk into a rocket factory, get the tour and then sit down with him. And he's got this big huge titanium desk or did at the time and uh we sat and talked and then walked around the factory for hours and just dove deep right away into a problem he was facing in manufacturing. >> What do you think he was assessing you on? >> He wanted to get a sense of like how I process problems. Um because when I asked him what success looked like, he said, "Oh, what success looks like is if you and I have the same inputs, we come up with the same answer." I thought that's pretty interesting. Um and I could sort of teased him about that. I said, "You because you're always right." And he said, he said, "Okay, fine. But I want to know just how you think through stuff." And so the best way for him to figure that out was let's go walk a real problem. >> What was the problem that you do you remember? They were having a hard time manufacturing the Model X uh Falcon Wing doors and and they've been working on this problem for weeks and uh not making any progress. And so we walked up and down the Model X line for the better part of two hours >> trying to figure out what was >> Yeah. Me just asking him questions like, "Okay, what where does misalign where does the chassis get built? how do you know it's aligned when it comes out? Where did the doors get hung on the chassis? And we saw something right away uh that he hadn't seen, which was the people that were bolting the doors onto the chassis, the Falcon Wing doors, had to do it blind. They were reaching around the underside and they had to like they had to drill these bolts in upside down and they couldn't see them. I was like, man, the chances of those things going in straight are pretty slow. It's pretty slim. have you ever thought about a jig? So that they could just follow a pattern. And he was like, "No, I haven't thought about that. Let's try that." So they literally built the jig overnight. Is that the thing with Elon that separates him from other people is like a lot of people would be like, "Oh, we'll do that next week. We'll >> Yeah. No, it's like the timing is as fast as you can." um because he believes that speed of all types, speed of decision-m, speed of cash through the business, speed of response time creates competitive advantage because your c your competitors are probably moving slower. >> How do you do that without burning people out? >> It's not every sec, every minute, every day you're on to something that requires immediate response. Like a lot of times you're trying to figure stuff out like how would we do this? How would we break down this problem? How would we grow this fast? Whatever. And then once you figure it out, you're going to hit the speed button for sure. But uh but it's not like you're constantly running at that rate. >> Did you know at that point you wanted to work at Tesla? >> It took some convincing because I hadn't I hadn't worked for somebody else for a long time. I had had six companies of my own. So, number one, I just wasn't sure I was ready to work for somebody else, and I wasn't sure that I was going to be helpful because the company was so big already and had such big growth goals. So, it really took some convincing on his part and really my part to figure out if that was if that was the right next step for me. My first concern, which sort of proved out in our first few weeks of interaction, was that I would overstep my bounds because I just wasn't used to having check-in with somebody. And turned out that I did. In my first two weeks, I overstepped oversteppet my pounds and it turned out not to be a fatal footfall. Uh, it was okay. >> What happened? >> I was trying to figure out if I could be helpful. And um, so I asked him like, "What's your biggest problem right now?" And he said, "Demand." And so I said, "Well, how many cars have you promised the street for this quarter?" And the number was something like 12,000. And we were a month and a half into the quarter at this point. And I said, "Well, how far in are you?" and he said, "We've only sold 3,000." And I was like, "Oh, that's a big problem." I said, "Okay, why don't I work on that problem for like a week and I'll come back?" And then I went out on a blitzkrieg. I went to eight different stores, took a test drive cuz I had heard that the test drive was the big thing in buying a Tesla. Like you hit the accelerator, it's like a rocket ship. You never forget it and you buy the car. So, I went to eight stores, did test drives, I used eight different email addresses so they wouldn't know who I was. And funny thing happened, I didn't get a call back. And after like a week, I hadn't been called back. So, I called the head of sales ops. I said, "Am I blacklisted in the system for some reason? Like, why would nobody call me back after a test drive? Cuz that is supposed to be when you're asking me for the sale." And he looked in the system. He said, "You're not blacklisted at all. you used a bunch of different email addresses so that we couldn't even track you basically. I said, "Well, can you look up for me how many people have done a test drive in the last 30 days who haven't been called back?" And he's like, "Yeah, give me an hour." So, he called me back uh and said like 10,000. And I'm like, "Oh my god, like you can make your number for the quarter. You just have to call people back and ask for the order. Why aren't people doing that?" And he said, "Well, people are incented to do test drives, but we have no incent. We have no commissions here, so they're not incented to make the sale." I said, "Yeah, the hardest thing in sales is asking for the sale. So, you're not incenting people to do that. I understand the behavior. So, why don't we do this? Can you shut off anybody's new test drive leads until they call all their prior test drives back for the last 30 days?" He's like, "I can't." I said, "Okay, how long will it take?" He's like, "Worldwide? Like, I can do it like right now. It'll take several hours uh to proliferate around the world, but I can do it right now. He called me the next day and he's like, "You wouldn't believe it. The orders are coming in left and right. It's" and I said, "Yeah, cuz you just your people are asking for the sale. This is how this works." And then I went, "Oh gosh, I don't work for Elon yet." And I just made a decision in his company. Like I shut off all new leads. So I called Elon and I said, "Hey, look, I'm really sorry. I haven't worked for anybody for a long time. And I was afraid of this and I just stepped across the line. And I told him what I did. I said, "Your problem in sales uh is that people aren't asking for the order." And so what I did was I shut off all new leads until they asked for the order. And it turns out the sales are coming in. I think you're going to make a quarter. I got to apologize to you though. I don't work for you yet. This isn't my company. It's yours. I should have checked in and I didn't. Just out of habit, I didn't check in and I'm sorry. And there was this long silence on the other end of the phone. And then he finally came on and he said, "That was a great decision. You're going to fit in here just fine." >> So he didn't mind you overstepping at all. >> Not in that case at all cuz it was speed of decision. Uh which I got to know was what he was after. He wasn't after a hierarchy or checking in. He was after as long as you're following first principles, just go as fast as you can. >> Do you remember what was going through your mind during that pause? >> Yeah. I thought first of all I didn't even know if he was on the phone still because uh it was it seemed like forever. It was probably less than a minute and literally I was asked ready to ask him were you still there when he uh when he jumped in. I got to know that that's how he processes. He kind of shuts down all other sensory stuff going on and just thinks that's what he was doing but I didn't know that on the other end of the phone. >> That would kind of freak me out. >> It freaked me out a little bit too. Yeah. >> How did you go about building a winning culture there? I think all culture comes from founders and the culture was was built and the culture was a first principles culture. It was a culture of rapid communication. So you didn't have to most organizations you go up the hierarchy with your question or your suggestion and it comes back down and it looks like an EKG the communication pattern in a company. Elon was like let's make it look like a dead patient. Go straight across the organization. If you need an answer go to the person that has that answer. don't go through their boss or their boss's boss, go directly to them because that's going to help with speed of decision-m so that kind of culture was already set. What the business needed was a bunch of scaffolding. So I went about building a team and then building approach so that we could have a mechanism to essentially double the company every 6 to 8 months like super rapid growth. And in so doing, we kind of built a culture. We built on the culture that Tesla already had. But we we really wanted to create a meritocracy where people that were contributing got big new assignments and we called them battlefield promotions. Like if you were if you were performing on the battlefield, we could literally grab you and say, "Hey, look, how would you like to run this worldwide?" And uh people would say, "I don't know how to do that." We'd say, "Well, nobody's ever done it before." So good. Welcome to the club. And we'd give them huge responsibilities, big remats, big assignments, and more often than not, they would come through and become fantastic leaders. >> What an incredible way to do that. >> Yeah. Yeah. It was super fun and still is cuz I still work with a number of those people today. >> What did you learn about communicating with Elon that was different? >> It has to be concise. And um and so we had this kind of fun we had fun with our communication in the sense that we gave each other a challenge. I don't know who came up with it. And uh I think it was his idea. He said, "Do you think we could we could try to run the organization on three sentence emails?" First sentence is here's my problem. Second sentence sentence is here's what I think the solution is. third sentence is here's my next step and if I need resources or permission ask in that sentence and so we we started to experiment with this and it was really the key to to communicating with him because he likes that sort of concise get to the point what's the have you super thought about the problem have you really thought about the solution and you thought about the next steps and that was kind of key to communicating with him the second key that he said all the time was don't sit on bad news give me bad news as fast as you know about it. And he said this to everybody. Um because bad news only gets worse with time. So like give me bad news fast. And the way that you could get on his on his bad side was saving bad news. And I watched that over time. Uh and so those were the two keys to communication like be concise and be rapid with bad news. >> How did you guys handle disagreements? >> We talked through them. Cheryl Samberg introduced us and so both of us quiz Cheryl on how do you and Mark manage your relationship and she said, "Okay, we meet once a week religiously for at least an hour. We open with here's here are here are things you've done that have pissed me off, frustrated me, uh disappointed me, whatever." So you clear all the good, you clear that stuff first and then you get to, oh, let's talk about the business strategy, whatever. So we sort of followed that and he's not shy. Like if he's upset about something, it's like right away the phone's lighting up. What the hell's going on? And I learned to be not shy, too. Uh, and it helped because I was a conflict avoider before Tesla and I'm definitely not a conflict avoider now. >> Wait, go deeper on that. >> I was more of a pleaser. loved to have teams that were productive and happy, but uh but I would wait on confrontation, especially if I was upset about something. And um and he didn't. And it taught me that was aokay because actually it's kind of the way a lot of organizations work outside of business. It's the way you know if you miss a note in an orchestra, the conductor is letting you know right away. Uh if you miss a play on the field, your coach is letting you know right away. And I started to appreciate that that was a very effective and helpful way to uh to keep a team learning rapidly. And you're talking about mistakes as much as you're talking about victories. >> A lot of people who who don't avoid the conflict don't necessarily say that in the most receptive way to other people. >> Right. Exactly. >> What have you learned about sort of communicating those messages to people as somebody who used to avoid it but now is trying to be more direct? I had a mentor who said, "If you're gonna, this is a kind of a coarse way of saying it, but he said, 'If you're going to slap somebody, they need a kiss, too." And so, I just learned to say, "Hey, look, I love working with you. I think you're super capable, but you you just failed in this moment or you're failing to solve this problem or you're failing to lead your team and I want to help you with that, but we have to address this." It is super harsh. I think to your point when you just leave it as, "Hey, you're failing and I'm so disappointed in you and you may not have your job." That's leaving somebody flapping. I'd rather say, "Hey, look, I respect you and I want to work I want to work you out of this, but you got to we got to get out of this uh whatever this tough tough spot is." >> And would would you be specific with that person? Oh, >> 100%. Yeah, because clarity really matters, I think, both on the positive side and on the negative side. If you're giving somebody feedback, you got to be super clear about here's what I'm pleased about. You did this super well. I watched you. Uh or you did this super not well. I watched you. How would you do this differently? Or let me give you some input how I think you probably should do it differently. We talked earlier about sort of how the sales people at Tesla weren't following up because they had no incentive to follow up. Yeah. I'm curious what you've learned about getting incentives right that you didn't know five years ago or 10 years ago. Yeah, I think I learned a lot from reading Charlie Mer uh and Charlie's this wisdom from Charlie that if you want to know how a system works, follow the incentives and and uh in that case there was a real incentive that was lacking and once you put that incentive in place now the incentive doesn't have to be monetary it can also be cultural and so Elon felt really strongly in that situation that we not have commissions because he wanted stores to be as opposite of car dealers as possible >> and you know when you go into a car dealership everybody's on commission and you feel that as the customer he did not want that feeling so then I the challenge was okay we as a team I as a leader have to figure out how are we going to get that behavior without a monetary reward and we stumbled across this thing we put a leaderboard up on every store and the leaderboard was number of sales that month and we drew a line almost arbitrarily in the middle of that chart and people would do a lot to get above that line even though nobody explained what the line was for. >> Exactly. It was just a well it was called, you know, the performance threshold or something like that. But there was no money involved. There was no commission. It was just, oh, I get it. The currency here is I need to not only give test drives, I need to sell cars. So that means I need to ask for the order. If I ask for the order, I move up that list. I'm above the line. I'm in the safety zone, whatever that meant. Um, and so it doesn't always need to be monetary, but you need to understand the incentives for sure. In that case, we created a non-monetary incentive. How did Elon think about risk? He thought, and I agree with this, he thought that the highest skill in business is allocating capital because as a capital allocator, you have to assess risk, assess it correctly. So, you're making a bet that ends up building your capital over time. And and so I started to think about that like poker. Um, oddly in every hand of poker, you can sort of run the math and understand whether you've got a bigger chance at upside or downside in that hand. And that then tells you how to bet. principles.title: Why I hate "deep" quotes
principles.content: The other day, I was innocently scrolling through Substack when I came across this quote attributed to the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. You should not be afraid of someone who has a library and reads many books. You should fear someone who has only one book and he considers it sacred, but he has never read it. It is a pretty pithy line. The only problem is that Nietzsche never said this and I think it totally misrepresents his critique of Christianity. This then sent me down a rabbit hole of googling some of my favorite thinkers and seeing what absolute nonsense has been attributed to them over the years and subsequently gone viral online. This video is the end result of that rabbit hole and what took me by surprise was just how often a quote would be genuine and still be highly misleading. My name is Joe Foley and this is unsolicited advice. One, philosophical quotes an imperfect taxonomy. Before getting into the broader reasons why I've come to dislike philosophical quotes really quite a lot, at least in how they're currently used, let's look at the species of philosophical quotes out there and broadly speaking I see them as falling into four camps which form a kind of quadrant based on A, whether the quote is real or fake, that is whether it is something the philosopher or thinker actually said and B, whether it is misleading or not. It'll become clearer what I mean by this as we go on. So first there are the quotes that are real but misleading and an absolutely extraordinary number of popular shared quotes fall into this camp. Let's take a classic one that I see passed around all the time attributed to Dostoevsky. The mystery of human existence lies not just in staying alive, but in finding something to live for. This is a real enough quote by Dostoevsky and it's in The Brothers Karamazov. This is not how it's translated in my copy, but it's a reasonable paraphrase of it and I'm sure it just comes from another translation. And at first glance it seems like a pretty inspirational quote. Surely this testifies to the fact that mankind has a deep need for existential meaning, and this is a sentiment that Dostoevsky himself would probably agree with. After all, he states in The House of the Dead that part of the torment of his imprisonment in Siberia and the prison labor was the sheer pointlessness of it all. And he argues that even a painless task like passing water between two empty glasses would be positively torturous if someone was made to do it endlessly in service to nothing. But of course, Dostoevsky is a novelist, and so many of the most famous quotations of his that seep into popular culture are actually spoken by his characters. So which character spoke this line? Well, it's none other than the villainous Grand Inquisitor, a symbol of tyranny and manipulation that represents how even for someone like Dostoevsky, who is deeply religious, Christianity can betray its original purpose and seize worldly power with which it can then dominate other men and come to even reject Christ in the process. As I've written about before, the Grand Inquisitor is something of Dostoevsky's near enemy. And as a result, he will often make statements that superficially resemble Dostoevsky's philosophy while also perverting it into something antithetical to his thought as a whole. In this case, we need only zoom out and look at the whole paragraph this quotation comes from to see the issue. And for context, the man the Grand Inquisitor is talking to is Jesus Christ. I tell you, man has no preoccupation more nagging than to find the person to whom that unhappy may surrender the gift of freedom with which he is born. But only he can take mastery of people's freedom who is able to set their consciences at rest. With bread, you were given an undisputed banner. Give bread, and man will bow down, for nothing is more undisputed than bread. But if at the same time someone takes mastery of his conscience without your knowledge, oh, then he will even throw down your bread and follow the one who seduces his conscience. In that you are right. For the secret of human existence does not consist in living merely, but in what one lives for. Without a firm idea of what he is to live for, man will not consent to live and will sooner destroy himself than remain on the earth, even though all around him there be loaves. That is so, but how's it worked out? Instead of taking mastery of people's freedom, you've increased that freedom even further. Or did you forget that peace of mind and even death are dearer to man than free choice and the cognition of good and evil. The exact meaning of this paragraph is clearer when reading the whole chapter, but in effect, the Grand Inquisitor is saying that it is kinder to mankind to take his freedom away and thus remove the burden of individual consciences. It's an argument for using political and religious authority to manipulate others into believing and acting how you, the despotic authority figure in question, please. This is placed in contrast to Christ, who the Grand Inquisitor says must not love mankind because Christ wanted their love to be freely given and for them to follow him out of that love rather than out of fear or deception or indebtedness. Within the context of the paragraph, the quotation has a very different meaning than is normally assumed. Out of context, it bears a passing resemblance to something Dostoevsky himself would say, but it does so by completely misrepresenting the work it comes from and the context within which the quotation is set. This is so commonplace with Dostoevsky quotes that get passed around the internet and there are even more egregious ones that outright invert his thought. Take the following one, for example. Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart. The really great men must, I think, have great sadness on earth. I see this quote passed around online an awful lot, but it is, and I you not, literally spoken by Raskolnikov as he is defending his theory that there are exceptional men separated from the rest of us who are permitted to break whatever public morality they please in their grand exceptionalness. It is explicitly part of a theory that Dostoevsky spends most of Crime and Punishment condemning. Arguably, if there is an argumentative through-line within Crime and Punishment, it is that the distinction between great men and the rest of us is really spurious and cannot be maintained.
